items.title: Anti-hawking laws pose potential threat to common referral practices
items.teaser: A core part of Financial Services Minister Dan Mulino’s tranche of reforms announced last month was a new anti-hawking regime, which will enhance consent requirements, limit the existing financial advice exemption to existing client relationships and strengthen penalties for breaches.
items.brief_text: A core part of Financial Services Minister Dan Mulino’s tranche of reforms announced last month was a new anti-hawking regime, which will enhance consent requirements, limit the existing financial advice exemption to existing client relationships and strengthen penalties for breaches. According to the changes, the current anti-hawking protections exemption are set to be limited to existing client relationships with the Government set to undertake consultations on targeted exemptions to ensure ‘low risk’ arrangements and necessary contact with family members and third parties of existing clients are protected. Restrictions will also be put in place banning unlicensed real-time communication with consumers about super as well as enhancing requirements around the consumers must give to enable real-time contact. There will, however, be targeted exceptions to protect advocacy, educational and employment communications. While much of this is seemingly targeted at cracking down on high-pressure sales tactics and lead-generation, the FAAA has highlighted that there could be unintended consequences that prevent advisers who are not applying high pressure sales tactics from contacting potential and prospective clients. “This is a really important issue, and it’s essential that the exemptions for financial advisers are appropriate and allow advisers to do what they need to do.

items.title: Why wasn’t Garry Crole permanently banned?
items.teaser: Effective from 4 September, Garry Crole was banned from performing as a director or responsible manager or any function involved in carrying on a financial services business, which ASIC said was a result of concerns related to his former roles as director and responsible manager of InterPrac Financial Planning.
items.brief_text: Effective from 4 September, Garry Crole was banned from performing as a director or responsible manager or any function involved in carrying on a financial services business, which ASIC said was a result of concerns related to his former roles as director and responsible manager of InterPrac Financial Planning. “ASIC found that Mr Crole was not a fit and proper person, was not competent, and lacked the diligence and judgement required to perform one or more functions as an officer of an entity carrying on a financial services business,” the regulator said. “ASIC found that Mr Crole was aware of serious concerns regarding the representatives’ financial advice model, which included the use of lead generators, and failed to adequately respond to these concerns. “ASIC also found that Mr Crole did not take adequate care in the management and oversight of InterPrac’s approved product list, which included First Guardian and Shield.” While the overall sentiment was support for the decision, the announcement was met with mixed responses. As expected, some were thoroughly pleased with the outcome, including an anonymised investor who commented: “I’ve been looking forward to this day! Thank you, ASIC.” Others argued that it will make no material impact on Crole or the circumstances surrounding the Shield and First Guardian mess as he had already resigned from Sequoia in July .

items.title: ART reviews five-year bans of two former advisers
items.teaser: Two former financial advisers have had their bannings reviewed by the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) over participating in flawed advice models.
items.brief_text: Two former financial advisers have had their bannings reviewed by the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) over participating in flawed advice models. Shane Monte Silva, formerly an authorised representative of FSGA and financial adviser at AS Financial Planning Pty Ltd, was initially banned by the regulator on 10 December 2025 after finding he had contravened financial services laws when providing superannuation switching advice to five clients. Andrew Hanley, banned March 2026, was an authorised representative of InterPrac Financial Planning and employed by Venture Egg, a partnership comprising Ferras Merhi Pty Ltd & United Financial Advice Pty Ltd and a corporate authorised representative of InterPrac. His application for orders preventing ASIC from publicising the decision was dismissed. Both were banned for five years from providing financial services. Fronting the ART on 7 September, the Tribunal affirmed ASIC’s initial decisions, finding that “both advisers participated in flawed advice models that failed to place clients’ interests first and resulted in inappropriate superannuation switching advice”. According to a statement by ASIC, the Tribunal identified “risks and deficiencies” in their respective advice models that “relied on unlicensed third-party telemarketers and paraplanners to perform key parts of the advice process”.

items.title: Review tribunal upholds Venture Egg, FSGA adviser bans
items.teaser: Shane Monte Silva, formerly an authorised representative of FSGA and financial adviser at AS Financial Planning Pty Ltd, was initially banned by the regulator on 10 December 2025 after finding he had contravened financial services laws when providing superannuation switching advice to five clients.
items.brief_text: Shane Monte Silva, formerly an authorised representative of FSGA and financial adviser at AS Financial Planning Pty Ltd, was initially banned by the regulator on 10 December 2025 after finding he had contravened financial services laws when providing superannuation switching advice to five clients. Andrew Hanley, banned March 2026, was an authorised representative of InterPrac Financial Planning and employed by Venture Egg, a partnership comprising Ferras Merhi Pty Ltd & United Financial Advice Pty Ltd and a corporate authorised representative of InterPrac. His application for orders preventing ASIC from publicising the decision was dismissed. Both were banned for five years from providing financial services. Fronting the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) on 7 September, the Tribunal affirmed ASIC’s initial decisions, finding that “both advisers participated in flawed advice models that failed to place clients’ interests first and resulted in inappropriate superannuation switching advice”. According to a statement by ASIC, the Tribunal identified “risks and deficiencies” in their respective advice models that “relied on unlicensed third-party telemarketers and paraplanners to perform key parts of the advice process”. “Under the models, advisers had little or no involvement in the initial fact-finding process and generally reviewed the advice only shortly before presenting it to clients,” the regulator explained.

items.title: Div 296 no hurdle to SMSF establishments, Class research finds
items.teaser: There’s never been more money in self-managed super funds than there is today, and the rate they’re being created has never been faster.
items.brief_text: More than 52,000 new SMSFs were established in FY26, the highest number ever recorded, according to new analysis by Class. The total number of funds surpassed 680,000, growth of 7.4 per cent on the year, also the highest total on record. Class chief executive Tim Steele says the growth has come despite Division 296 and new limits on residential property borrowing. “Firstly, I would say at a macro level, SMSFs have just had the strongest year on record,” Steele says. “Despite the kind of regulatory backdrop and potentially changes in relation to things like Div 296, SMSFs are more popular than they’ve ever been.” “The themes around control and flexibility, and people taking an interest and being engaged in their super, are already positive things,” Steele says. Steele says the Div 296 tax change has not deterred even younger members who may cross the $3 million threshold over their working lives. “I think it’s a problem they’d love to have,” Steele says. “When someone age 21 enters the workforce and is contributing 12.5 per cent of their super, that beautiful eighth wonder of the world, compound interest, will mean they can grow a material balance over their lifetime. “I just don’t think the potential risk of, at some stage in your life, having more than $3 million in super, is a deterrent.

items.title: Tribunal affirms ASIC ban on advisers at the centre of Shield and First Guardian failed advice
items.teaser: The Administrative Review Tribunal has affirmed the five-year bans imposed by ASIC on financial advisers Andrew Hanley and Shane Monte Silva for their role in switching clients’ superannuation to Shield and First Guardian without proper assessment.
items.brief_text: The five-year ban imposed by the Australian Securities and Investment Commission on former Venture Egg financial adviser Andrew Hanley and FSGA adviser Shane Monte Silva has been confirmed by the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) on 7 September. In December 2025, ASIC banned Monte Silva for contravening financial services laws when advising five clients to move their superannuation. The five-year ban, which prevents him from providing financial services, was publicly announced in April 2026. Monte Silva applied for a review with the ART. “The Applicant’s conduct has damaged the public’s confidence in, and the integrity of, the financial market relating to superannuation,” the ART said. “He engaged in misleading and deceptive conduct and continued to participate in an advice-giving model despite knowing that it was flawed. “A reasonable and competent financial adviser would have stepped aside and stopped giving the flawed advice. His failure to do so demonstrated a disregard for the law and compliance with regulations.” The decision was based on advice provided by Monte Silva between July and August 2023 to roll their existing superannuation into platforms with substantial investments in Shield and First Guardian. The ART found he was not involved in gathering client information, had limited time to assess client’s circumstances and relied on information provided by others.

items.title: Victims’ advocate says Crole banning ‘best thing ASIC has done’
items.teaser: A leading advocate for investors in the collapsed Shield and First Guardian master funds has welcomed the banning of the former chief executive of the licensee at the centre of investor losses.
items.brief_text: Shield and First Guardian victims’ advocate Melinda Kee says the 10-year ban of former InterPrac managing director Garry Crole, announced by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission on Tuesday, is “one of the best things I think ASIC has done”. ASIC has banned Crole, who stepped down as Sequoia Financial Group chief executive on 22 July but remains a substantial shareholder in the beleaguered ASX-listed wealth management group, from performing, as a director or responsible manager, any function involved in carrying on a financial services business. ASIC said it found that Crole was not a fit and proper person, was not competent, and lacked the diligence and judgement required to perform one or more functions as an officer of an entity carrying on a financial services business. It said InterPrac authorised representatives Venture Egg and Rhys Reilly advised thousands of clients to invest their superannuation in the First Guardian and Shield master funds, which both subsequently collapsed. It found that Crole was “aware of serious concerns regarding the representatives’ financial advice model, which included the use of lead generators, and failed to adequately respond to these concerns”. ASIC also found that Crole did not take adequate care in the management and oversight of InterPrac’s approved product list, which included First Guardian and Shield. “They hit the nail on the head. They absolutely hit the nail on the head,” Kee tells Professional Planner .

items.title: Planned new home builds will be cancelled
items.teaser: Hogan said off-the-plan apartment projects depend on SMSF buyers for early presales and without them, developers won’t get finance and the homes will never be built. “Labor has banned self-managed super funds from borrowing to buy residential property, including new builds.
items.brief_text: Hogan said off-the-plan apartment projects depend on SMSF buyers for early presales and without them, developers won’t get finance and the homes will never be built. “Labor has banned self-managed super funds from borrowing to buy residential property, including new builds. This isn’t rocket science,” Hogan said. “Banning SMSFs from borrowing to buy new houses and apartments will only result in fewer homes being built. The Government seems to have not bothered to do the analysis. If they want to be taken seriously on super, they should at least model the impact of their changes.” Hogan said Treasury has confirmed under Freedom of Information that no regulatory impact statement was prepared. “There is no modelling and no analysis of the consequences. The Government said the measure would affect around 4,000 loans a year. Industry says more than 16,000 SMSF residential loans were written in the year to June alone,” Hogan said. “In their Budget, Labor already admitted their taxes would result in 35,000 fewer homes being built. This change just adds to their anti-housing agenda.” Hogan continued the Government is targeting SMSFs and has in the past five months changed rules governing the sector four times. “In March, the Division 296 super tax passed Parliament after three separate designs across three years: unrealised gains in, unrealised gains out, thresholds unindexed, then indexed, one tier, then two. SMSF investors are disproportionately hit by this tax,” he said.

items.title: Tribunal affirms InterPrac, FSGA adviser bans
items.teaser: The Administrative Review Tribunal has affirmed ASIC's decisions to ban two former financial advisers from InterPrac Financial Planning and Financial Services Group Australia (FSGA) who were involved in the Shield and First Guardian master funds for five years.
items.brief_text: The Administrative Review Tribunal has affirmed ASIC's decisions to ban two former financial advisers from InterPrac Financial Planning and Financial Services Group Australia (FSGA) who were involved in the Shield and First Guardian master funds for five years. Andrew Hanley and Shane Monte Silva received their verdicts after applying to the tribunal to review their respective five-year bans. Hanley was an authorised representative of InterPrac between 28 March 2023 and 15 August 2024 and worked within the Venture Egg advice model. The tribunal found that Hanley failed to act in the best interests of at least six clients and provided inappropriate advice. He advised four clients to invest in First Guardian, while advising two other clients to switch to Venture Egg model portfolios. "Hanley had little or no interaction with the relevant clients or input into the preparation of the advice. He generally had only minutes to review the advice and assess its adequacy before joining calls to present it to clients," ASIC said. Separately, Monte Silva was an authorised representative of FSGA from 24 May 2023 to 10 March 2025. He was found to have advised five clients to roll their super into platforms and invest in Shield and First Guardian between July and August 2023. FSGA is currently in liquidation.

items.title: FAAA warns CSLR bill could hit before Christmas
items.teaser: Already this year, CSLR costs have skyrocketed.
items.brief_text: Already this year, CSLR costs have skyrocketed. The 2026/27 financial year CSLR levy estimated total came out to $198.1 million , the majority of which ($190.3 million) has been attributed to the financial advice sector, creating a $170.3 million overflow that needs to be dealt with through a special levy due to the $20 million subsector cap. Running an advice business is an expensive exercise as it is, with compliance costs, ASIC fees, high wages and technology fees, but advisers should expect these costs to run even higher if the FAAA’s prediction of a pre-Christmas gift is true. “Our expectation is that the government in the next few weeks will bring forward its determination on the special levy, and that it’s likely to go through this year. So, the payment of the levy may well occur at the end of this year or early next year,” Andrea Forbes, FAAA government relations consultant said. “The reason why the government are doing that is they’re very conscious that they want to get the victims of these collapses, they want to get their money to them more quickly as well. So that’s just something to look out for.” Forbes added that currently, the FAAA is arguing that this special levy number should be zero. “What we are advocating for with the 2026–27 levy is zero.

items.title: SMSFs continue to take away from APRA-based funds
items.teaser: Colin Williams, Wealth Data Manager, Padura, said the latest APRA data for the June 2026 quarter show industry funds continue to “bleed money” to SMSFs, though at a slower pace than the recent run of accelerating losses. “The underlying trend continues, but the pace of deterioration has slowed,” Williams said.
items.brief_text: Colin Williams, Wealth Data Manager, Padura, said the latest APRA data for the June 2026 quarter show industry funds continue to “bleed money” to SMSFs, though at a slower pace than the recent run of accelerating losses. “The underlying trend continues, but the pace of deterioration has slowed,” Williams said. “The rolling annual net transfer from industry funds to SMSFs eased further into negative territory, from –$7.76 billion (year to March 2026) to –$7.87 billion (year to June 2026) — still a record low, but the quarter-on-quarter worsening (+$0.11 billion) was far smaller than the +$0.55 billion deterioration seen in the previous quarter. “The single June quarter saw industry funds shed –$1.58 billion to SMSFs, an improvement on March’s –$1.91 billion and continuing to ease from the back-to-back record quarters of –$2.21 billion and –$2.17 billion recorded in late 2025. However, the quarter net outflow of $1.58 billion was greater than the previous June 2025 quarter of $1.48 billion.” The APRA data also revealed that retail funds have been steadily building with the key measure being the “net transfer” of funds between all fund types. “In simple terms, the net position of all funds that were transferred in and out to other funds. Retail funds have now gone nine straight quarters of positive net gains. In the previous 25 quarters, it only had three positive quarters,” Williams noted.

items.title: Named, but not accused: ASIC’s warning that isn’t a warning
items.teaser: When ASIC warns consumers to take care when dealing with a service provider but doesn’t explain to them why, it does not support informed decision-making. The information published should be sufficiently precise to let the reader understand what is known and what is not and why the warning has been issued.
items.brief_text: Imagine that your business appears on a consumer warning page published by ASIC. The page tells consumers to exercise “additional caution”. It sits within a regulatory campaign prompted by concerns that Australians are being pressured into switching their superannuation and exposed to significant losses. ASIC announces your inclusion in a media release and says it is putting industry participants “on notice”. But ASIC also says that naming your business should not be understood as indicating that any law has been broken, or even as reflecting upon you. What, then, is the public supposed to make of your name being on this list? That is the unresolved contradiction at the centre of ASIC’s list of businesses involved in superannuation lead generation. The List ASIC began publishing ‘the list’ in February 2026 as part of a review of advice licensees using lead-generation services. It initially named 44 entities and added another 19 in June. The list includes lead generators and referral partners, as well as advice licensees, corporate authorised representatives and financial advisers that have acquired leads since 1 July 2024. ASIC says some lead-generation practices may expose consumers to significant losses. Its accompanying warnings refer to high-pressure tactics, “free” superannuation health checks, claims that existing funds are underperforming, limited contact with an adviser, poor product disclosure and promises of unrealistic returns.

items.title: Treasury floats innovative businesses CGT concession draft laws
items.teaser: Treasury has released draft legislation on a capital gains tax (CGT) concession for start-ups and small businesses, embedding several amendments that have been lauded as a "substantial win" by an industry body.
items.brief_text: Treasury has released draft legislation on a capital gains tax (CGT) concession for start-ups and small businesses, embedding several amendments that have been lauded as a "substantial win" by an industry body. From 1 July 2027, the bill introduces a 50% CGT discount for investors who back eligible innovative Australian start-up companies. For an entity to be eligible to apply the CGT discount on an Innovative Business CGT Concession (IBCC) asset, the entity must have chosen to apply the discount rather than cost-base indexation. The entity must also not be a company, complying superannuation entity or foreign resident, as these entities have different CGT arrangements. The new law defines an IBCC company as one that develops a "genuinely innovative product, process service or method," is incorporated for less than 15 years, based in Australia and is not controlled by another company that has been incorporated for 15 or more years. It must not be listed and must have annual turnover below $50 million. The Tech Council of Australia (TCA) said the most significant change is the removal of the lifetime cap. "TCA has strongly advocated for changes to the cap limit so that founders remain properly incentivised to take on the risk of starting high-growth tech companies. "Employees will also have stronger incentives to join tech startups in their early years.

items.title: ART upholds ban on former financial advisers
items.teaser: ART found that Andrew Hanley and Shane Monte Silva participated in flawed advice models that failed to place clients’ interests first and resulted in inappropriate superannuation switching advice.
items.brief_text: ART found that Andrew Hanley and Shane Monte Silva participated in flawed advice models that failed to place clients’ interests first and resulted in inappropriate superannuation switching advice. It found that Hanley failed to act in the best interests of six clients and provided advice that was not appropriate to their circumstances. Four clients were advised to invest in First Guardian, while two were advised to switch to Venture Egg model portfolios. Hanley was an authorised representative of Interprac Financial Planning Pty Ltd and worked within the Venture Egg advice model. The ART found that Hanley had little or no interaction with the relevant clients or input into the preparation of the advice. He generally had only minutes to review the advice and assess its adequacy before joining calls to present it to clients. In regard to Monte Silva, the ART found that between July and August 2023, Monte Silva, while an authorised representative of Financial Services Group Australia (in liquidation) (FSGA), advised five clients to roll their existing superannuation into platforms with substantial investments in Shield and First Guardian. Furthermore, it found that Monte Silva had no involvement in gathering key client information, had limited opportunity to assess clients’ circumstances and often saw Statements of Advice only shortly before presenting them to clients.

items.title: APRA simplifies retirement data collection by trustees
items.teaser: As part of its response to industry feedback on the proposed Retirement Reporting Framework, the prudential regulator has streamlined data requirements, ensuring transparency while reducing the excessive data collection burden.
items.brief_text: As part of its response to industry feedback on the proposed Retirement Reporting Framework, the prudential regulator has streamlined data requirements, ensuring transparency while reducing the excessive data collection burden. The framework is part of the government's retirement phase reforms, intended to improve understanding of how trustees support members in navigating retirement. APRA kicked off the consultation early in the year to effectively collect and report data from superannuation funds as part of its work under the Retirement Income Covenant. Treasurer Jim Chalmers released the reforms to help put as much focus on the retirement phase as there is in the accumulation phase. APRA's role is to collect and publish the data every year from 2027 to produce and deliver insights on fund offerings and member outcomes and to help track progress with retirement phase uplift. Most stakeholders encouraged APRA to consider whether the level of granularity in the proposed collection was proportionate to the policy objectives of the retirement reporting framework. In response, APRA has substantially reduced reporting granularity, while preserving the information necessary to support the government's indicators. "APRA considers the revised approach better balances transparency, comparability and proportionality, and is more closely aligned to the intended purpose of the Retirement Reporting Framework," APRA said.

items.title: First Super appoints new chief executive
items.teaser: First Super has appointed a new chief executive who was part of LUCRF Super's leadership team for 18 years.
items.brief_text: First Super has appointed a new chief executive who was part of LUCRF Super's leadership team for 18 years. Tim Kennedy will commence in the new role on October 5. He recently served as the national secretary of the United Workers Union (UWU), which represents 150,000 workers from across from more than 45 industries, working in sectors such as health, aged care, early education, security, manufacturing and hospitality. Kennedy also led the National Union of Workers, which merged with United Voice to create the United Workers Union in November 2019. Kennedy is the former chair and deputy chair, as well as director of LUCRF Super and served in those roles between 2004 and 2022. He served on the investment committee for over a decade and chaired the audit and risk committee. LUCRF Super officially merged into AustralianSuper in June 2022. LUCRF Super had $7.25 billion in funds under management and about 130,000 members. Kennedy steps into the role currently filled in the interim by Greg Everett, following the resignation of chief executive Bill Watson in early January. Watson resigned from the post after about 13 years, having joined from business advisory firm Evans & Peck. Watson joined BUSSQ as chief investment officer in April. Greg Everett became the acting chief executive in March, having served as deputy chief executive.

items.title: ‘Doesn’t cut the mustard’: Equity Trustees defends apparent governance breakdown
items.teaser: Appearing before a joint parliamentary committee on 10 September, Michael O’Brien, managing director of Equity Trustees and non-executive director Catherine Robson defended the trustees’ conduct in relation to Shield and First Guardian.
items.brief_text: Appearing before a joint parliamentary committee on 10 September, Michael O’Brien, managing director of Equity Trustees and non-executive director Catherine Robson defended the trustees’ conduct in relation to Shield and First Guardian. But early on in the proceedings it was revealed that New Quantum sent an email in March 2022 requesting that Equity Trustees Superannuation Limited (ETSL) add the high growth class of the Shield Master Fund to NQ Super’s approved product list (APL) with a 95 per cent holding limit. “One of your employees, and I’m not going to mention their names, from the superannuation investment office of ETSL, contacts an employee at the superannuation trustee office and says, ‘This request has been approved. It’s submitted for approval. If you’d like to discuss, please contact us’,” Senator Paul Scarr said. “And the response that they get, and this is in paragraph 84 of the pleading from the superannuation trustee office, to increase this holding limit from 50 per cent to 95 per cent in a high growth fund is: ‘Thanks. Easy peasy. Done’.” O’Brien argued this was an “unfortunate turn of phrase” and that the group does have a “well-developed investment governance framework”, adding that it was followed on that occasion.

items.title: One Nation ‘super pay boost’ at odds with adequacy, retirement plans
items.teaser: As new research reveals more than a third of Australians want a superannuation retirement balance of $1.25 million or more, One Nation has unveiled a plan to allow workers pocket 3 per cent of their super contributions, which could leave them tens of thousands of dollars short of their target.
items.brief_text: As new research from MLC reveals that 35 per cent of Australians want at least $1.25 million in superannuation by the time they retire, a One Nation proposal to allow Australians to take home 3 per cent of their compulsory super has been attacked for potentially undermining retirement savings adequacy. One Nation has proposed that members paying rent or a mortgage would have the choice to take home one quarter of the compulsory 12 per cent Superannuation Guarantee (SG) contributions employers pay to their employees’ super, for a maximum period of three years. The party also proposed this would not be taxed as part of ordinary wages, but as if it were going into employees’ super accounts. The rationale that a full-time worker earning $90,500 would have an extra $2300 a year and a couple making $168,000 would have $4300 after tax is at odds with the findings from MLC and what AFSA recommends. The MLC research released on Sunday divides the expected superannuation in three categories: modest, luxe and champagne. Modest retirement includes activities from sports to camping as well as eating out locally every few weeks, annual domestic holidays and a few overseas trips over the course of their retirement. “Whereas a ‘Luxe retirement’ includes weekly meals out, more international travel, and more freedom,” says Renee Howie, MLC chief customer officer.

items.title: Hewison departure will open door to ‘fresh voice, ideas, enthusiasm’
items.teaser: Second-generation Hewison Private Wealth managing director Andrew Hewison tells Professional Planner there will be no changes to the business and no clients will be affected as a result of Pemba Capital Partners’ investment, followed by his departure at the end of the year.
items.brief_text: Hewison Private Wealth soon-to-depart managing director Andrew Hewison has assured staff and clients there will be no changes to the business as it takes on external investment from Pemba Capital Partners. “In fact, there’ll be greater opportunities in the future for our advisers to become owners and shareholders in the business. And some of our smaller shareholders are actually increasing their ownership in the business along with Pemba,” Hewison tells Professional Planner . He first shared his decision to leave the firm with major shareholders and board members in 2024, to ensure the business had ample time to make a succession plan. He explains that he felt “like the time was right for me to step aside, introduce a fresh voice, fresh enthusiasm, fresh ideas into the business to take it to the next phase. But ultimately, it remains a continuation of our current strategy”. Hewison says he will step away from all operational involvement and act as a non-executive director. A search for his replacement is currently underway. One of the main questions clients have been asking after Hewison announced he will be stepping down from the business at the end of 2026 is “is my adviser leaving?”, and the answer is no, according to him. Pemba has a non-operational stake in the firm and will take board seats for strategic reasons, but it doesn’t want to upset a successful business, according to Hewison.

items.title: Unisuper deepens advice capabilities with head appointment
items.teaser: This comes as the Government has essentially greenlit the large superfunds too invest deeper in their financial advice capabilities following the announcement of the implementation of the ‘New Class of Adviser’ regime.
items.brief_text: This comes as the Government has essentially greenlit the large superfunds too invest deeper in their financial advice capabilities following the announcement of the implementation of the ‘New Class of Adviser’ regime. “Advice has the power to change lives, not just finances – and it’s one of the many reasons I was attracted to this opportunity,” Slade said of her appointment. “I’m looking forward to continuing to build on the strong foundation already in place at UniSuper – shaping the future of advice through strategic thinking, strong governance, technical excellence and innovation, all with a focus on delivering better outcomes for members.” Slade joins Unisuper after just over a decade at TelstraSuper, where she held a number of senior roles. These included head of retirement, product and CX risk, head of member services, regional manager Victoria and manager, limited advice. Prior to this, she spent 10 years as team manager of advice and engagement at First State Super and a short stint at Superpartners as team leader of financial education and advice team. Before making her way into the superannuation world, Slade also worked as a financial adviser; first as a paraplanner and then a financial planner at Outlook Financial Solutions and later at Professional Alliance Financial Planning and Risk. “As I start this next chapter, I’d also like to thank the many people in my network who generously shared their time, insights and connections with me over the past few months.

items.title: Lower pension spending should not be the sole measure of retirement success
items.teaser: Richard Webb, CPA Australia Superannuation Lead, said Australia risks focusing too heavily on reducing Age Pension costs rather than ensuring retirees enjoy adequate retirement incomes.
items.brief_text: Richard Webb, CPA Australia Superannuation Lead, said Australia risks focusing too heavily on reducing Age Pension costs rather than ensuring retirees enjoy adequate retirement incomes. Webb said comments from Treasurer Jim Chalmers at the Super Members Council (SMC) Super Summit on Wednesday, 9 September, highlighting Australia’s projected decline in pension spending compared with other developed economies overlooks a fundamental difference between retirement systems. “The real test of a retirement system is whether it delivers dignity, security and adequate incomes in retirement,” he said “New Zealand’s recent proposal to increase KiwiSaver contributions to 12 per cent, matching Australia’s Superannuation Guarantee, highlights the different paths being taken by the two countries. “New Zealand is moving towards the same compulsory savings rate as Australia, but its pension system operates very differently. Unlike Australia, they don’t subject most retirees to complex means testing before they can access the state pension.” Webb said universal access to NZ Super (the Aged Pension equivalent) provides retirees with greater certainty when planning for retirement. “In Australia, retirees can spend decades building their superannuation balances only to face a complex interaction between superannuation, income tests and asset tests when they retire.

items.title: PPS Mutual Appoints Senior BDM in Victoria

items.brief_text: PPS Mutual has appointed Voula Makris as Senior Business Development Manager for Victoria, reporting to Shadia Kouzma, the State Manager. The company says in her new role Makris will drive growth across Victoria, working with PPS Mutual’s accredited adviser network to strengthen risk insurance capability, support sustainable practice development and help advisers deliver high-quality protection

items.title: Russell launches retirement solution
items.teaser: Russell Investments has launched retirement solutions comprising two managed portfolios and a retirement calculator, aimed at helping advisers manage the competing liquidity and growth needs of Australians entering retirement.
items.brief_text: Russell Investments has launched retirement solutions comprising two managed portfolios and a retirement calculator, aimed at helping advisers manage the competing liquidity and growth needs of Australians entering retirement. The solution allows advisers to structure retirement assets across three-time horizons: near-term spending and liquidity, future income needs and longer-term capital growth. It includes the Russell Investments Short-Term and Medium- Term Portfolios, alongside an appropriate long-term growth portfolio and a purpose-built retirement calculator. Russell Investments head of distribution Australia and New Zealand Neil Rogan said retirement should not be treated as a single investment phase. He added that an estimated 2.5 million Australian's are expected to retire over the next decade, while people paged 65 can expect to live for more than 20 additional years on average, citing government data. "Pre- and post-retirement is not a single investment phase. Clients still need long-term growth, but they are also drawing from their portfolio to fund their everyday living expenses," Rogan said. "The challenge for advisers is balancing the money clients need to live on today with the assets that need to remain invested for the years ahead. Our Retirement Solution provides a framework for managing those competing needs." The Short-Term Portfolio focuses on income and capital stability, while the Medium-Term Portfolio invests across income and moderate growth assets.

items.title: Akumin wants to support ambitious quality firms
items.teaser: Akumin has welcomed firms with as few as two advisers to more than 100 in 2026, CEO Matt Lawler tells Professional Planner that the licensee’s growth strategy is focused on the ambitions and quality of potential target firms, not their size.
items.brief_text: Akumin has had at least two financial planning businesses join the AFSL in 2026, one with more than 120 advisers and another with just two staff in their financial planning business. Akumin CEO Matt Lawler tells Professional Planner that the licensee’s growth strategy is focused on the ambitions and quality of potential target firms, not their size. “We’re at our best when we’re working with quality firms that have ambitions. [Firms] that want to grow, that are not happy with where they are today, and they’re eager to evolve. That’s probably where we’re at our best,” Lawler says. “And if there are businesses out there that do have ambitions, and that could be to grow, it could be succession planning, it could be to add new services, it could be to increase the number of clients they look after, mergers, acquisitions. We’re well equipped to look after all of those, assist firms with all of those ambitions.” Aperio Financial Services has joined the Akumin AFSL with plans to grow its financial advice services while receiving support from Akumin around recruitment, paraplanning, technology and marketing. Since joining Akumin in February, Aperio has already added one person to its financial planning business, purchased a new Melbourne office, hired five new accounting staff and has plans to add at least another 15 staff to the business.

items.title: Integro and Coastline merger a vote of confidence in the value of risk advice
items.teaser: The merger of Coastline Private Wealth with fellow WA-based financial advice firm Integro Private Wealth is a vote of confidence by Integro in the value of risk advice, its partner and private wealth adviser Justin Gilmour says.
items.brief_text: Perth-based Integro Private Wealth’s merger with fellow WA firm Coastline Private Wealth will enable the combined entity to build a separate risk advice division that sits alongside its wealth management business and bring scale to its insurance offer, Integro partner Justin Gilmour says. Gilmour tells Professional Planner that as advisers continue to desert the risk market, and as that sector undergoes continued aggregation, “it’s a time to lean in”. “It’s more challenging in that space now to operate, so we really want to build out a division on that risk side without diluting the value of the wealth side. He says Integro’s risk service has always met client needs but “it’s not as proactive as what we’d like, and also it’s something where, with risk premiums going through the roof in terms of pricing, it’s a really good opportunity to be a specialist in that market and rather than [taking] sort of a cookie cutter approach, do it properly”. Gilmour says a properly constructed wealth plan should eliminate the need for insurance over time. “At each review with the client, we would be doing updated financial modelling to show the client where they’re tracking… back against those objectives,” he says. “So, as wealth increases, we want to make the risk redundant as quick as we can. It’s purely around what the need is at the time, and as they reach, or they get closer to, financial independence, the need for the risk [insurance] would diminish.

items.title: CFS swops Platypus for Firetrail after boutique’s closure
items.teaser: Firetrail Investments has been appointed to run an Australian equities strategy for CFS, previously run by Platypus Asset Management. It was announced at the start of September by parent company Australian Unity that it would be winding down Platypus from 28 September.
items.brief_text: Firetrail Investments has been appointed to run an Australian equities strategy for CFS, previously run by Platypus Asset Management. It was announced at the start of September by parent company Australian Unity that it would be winding down Platypus from 28 September. Founded in 1998, Platypus Asset Management entered a joint venture with Australian Unity in 2006 which then moved to full ownership in 2022. The firm said it had “considered a variety of different options” for Platypus and concluded that ownership of the fund manager no longer aligned with its strategy for the Wealth and Capital Markets business. It also said Platypus faced “long-term profitability and viability challenges” due to the evolving environment for Australian equity fund managers. In light of this, CFS has appointed boutique fund manager Firetrail to manage its Platypus Australian Equities investment option and the option name will change to the Firetrail High Conviction Australian equities strategy. The new Firetrail option aims to deliver strong returns through a predominantly concentrated portfolio of Australian shares against the S&P/ASX 200 benchmark. Both Firetrail and Platypus run the strategies with a high conviction focus on Australian equities, a suggested seven-year timeframe and 90-100 per cent invested in shares. This transition is expected to be completed in late September and Firetrail will formally take over management of the portfolio.

items.title: Housing package estimated to cut 10,700 homes and push rents higher: new modelling
items.teaser: The Master Builders Australia, Housing Industry Association, Property Council of Australia, and the REIA released updated independent modelling of the Federal Budget housing package.
items.brief_text: The Master Builders Australia, Housing Industry Association, Property Council of Australia, and the REIA released updated independent modelling of the Federal Budget housing package. The modelling examines the cumulative impact of the Federal Budget’s primary housing tax reforms, including changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax concession arrangements, together with the $2 billion Housing Support Program. The updated modelling incorporates the additional measure agreed by Labor and the Greens during negotiations to secure passage of the broader package through Parliament that prohibits SMSFs from using LRBAs to purchase ordinary residential investment property. The analysis by Qaive and Tulipwood Economics finds that between 2026–27 and 2029–30, the combined housing measures are estimated to reduce new dwelling starts by 10,700, increase rents by approximately $10 per week, reduce cumulative GDP by approximately $1.05 billion; and cut construction jobs by more than 4,700. The findings represent a further deterioration from the modelling released immediately after the Budget, which already showed that the package would reduce housing construction, weaken economic activity, and place additional pressure on renters. The housing industry bodies said the updated figures reinforce that Australia cannot resolve its housing shortage through policies that make it harder to finance, build, and supply rental homes.

items.title: Russell Investments partners with CFS for two managed portfolios
items.teaser: Russell Investments is launching two new retirement solutions on CFS Edge as more Australians move into retirement, and life expectancy lifts. The investment firm points to “competing needs” for individuals between having to plan for longer lives and accessing money before retirement.
items.brief_text: Russell Investments is launching two new retirement solutions on CFS Edge as more Australians move into retirement, and life expectancy lifts. The investment firm points to “competing needs” for individuals between having to plan for longer lives and accessing money before retirement. Russell Investments also notes demographic changes, estimating that around 2.5 million people are expected to retire in Australia within the next decade. Further, Australian Government data shows that in average, people aged 65 can expect to live longer lives than their predecessors. To address these challenges, Russell Investments offers a new mix of portfolios for advisers to manage clients’ assets in the short, medium and long term. The two new managed portfolios are the ‘Russell Investments Short-Term’ and ’Russell Medium-Term’. They are completed by a long-term growth portfolio and a purpose-built ‘Retirement Calculator.’ According to Russell Investments, the Short-Term Portfolio focuses on income and capital stability, while the Medium-Term Portfolio invests across income and moderate growth assets. “Advisers can use the new Short-Term and Medium-Term Portfolios, while retaining a suitable existing portfolio for long-term growth,” read a company statement. Neil Rogan, head of distribution ANZ at Russell Investments, added: “Clients still need long-term growth, but they are also drawing from their portfolio to fund their everyday living expenses.

items.title: Brilliant, reckless and not a paraplanner
items.teaser: Imagine a new hire who gets it wrong once in every five jobs. Not in a way you would catch on a quick read.
items.brief_text: Imagine a new hire who gets it wrong once in every five jobs. Not in a way you would catch on a quick read. Wrong in a way that reads beautifully, quotes a threshold with total assurance and turns out to be invented. You would supervise that person closely. Most practices have brought exactly that capability into the advice process without deciding who supervises it. Worth saying early: nothing here suggests the technology replaces paraplanners. The hours it saves are real and worth taking. The question is what happens to the output before it reaches a client. How often the tools get it wrong Research cited by the European Securities and Markets Authority found ChatGPT fabricating content in about 19.5 per cent of responses. That work dates from 2023 so the models have improved since. The behaviour behind it has not. Testing published by the United Kingdom consumer body Which? in July this year put 15 personal finance questions to five widely used chat tools and scored them between 60 and 68 per cent. The failures matter more than the scores. ChatGPT invented a savings product that does not exist and pointed users to a pensions body that had already closed. Copilot and Google’s overviews quoted capital gains tax rates that stopped applying in October 2024. Several tools answered United Kingdom questions with United States rules. The difficulty is not that these systems fail. It is that they fail without any change in tone.

items.title: Liquidity divide: Why retirees hold back from guaranteed income
items.teaser: The 2026 AMP Retirement Confidence Pulse found 84 per cent of Australians said guaranteed income for life would help them spend more confidently in retirement but uptake isn’t matching that.
items.brief_text: The 2026 AMP Retirement Confidence Pulse found 84 per cent of Australians said guaranteed income for life would help them spend more confidently in retirement but uptake isn’t matching that. Even clients who see the appeal hesitate once they understand what they’re giving up, according to Jordan Vaka, founder of Planning Solo. “People want guaranteed income, but they’re not comfortable with the downsides or the perceived downsides that come with that guaranteed income,” Vaka told ifa. The products tie up significant capital to maximise Centrelink benefits, and that’s where the real friction sits. There is real uptake in one group, Vaka explained, as clients with a paid-off home, reasonable super, and still qualifying for the age pension are willing to lock money into guaranteed products because, for them, it makes sense. Divorced or separated clients approach retirement carefully. “Their life’s been torn apart,” Vaka said. “It’s completely different than what they were expecting.” Women in this cohort are familiar with the statistics around homelessness and financial risk, so they hold onto access to their money because they’ve lost control once already. They’re not letting it happen again. They need certainty they can access cash if costs spike. Widow clients are often in a stronger financial position, he said, but they need liquidity for different reasons.

items.title: Asset-based fees dwindle as firms price for complexity, not wealth
items.teaser: New research has found that the shift away from asset-based fees is gathering pace, with advice fees increasingly being based on the complexity of the client, not on portfolio size.
items.brief_text: Asset-based fees are losing their grip on financial advice pricing, with the size of a client’s portfolio having significantly less influence on what advisers charge now than it did three years ago, new research has found. Vital Business Partners’ 2026 Advice Fee Benchmarking Report , based on a confidential survey of 143 advice firms representing about 500 advisers and conducted in the first quarter of 2026, finds that pricing now increasingly follows the complexity of a client’s affairs and rewards the adviser’s professional judgement and expertise, not assets under advice. Firms were asked how they price their services generally, and what they would charge to advise five hypothetical clients ranging from a young couple with a mortgage to a high-net-worth family with $12.5 million in assets. The report says the proportion of firms charging a purely asset-based ongoing fee “has fallen from 18 per cent in 2023 to 10 per cent in 2026,” a decline of 8 percentage points, or 44 per cent. The report says fixed fees are now “the most commonly used pricing model for ongoing advice services,” adopted by 49 per cent of firms. Hybrid structures, which combine a fixed fee with a percentage component , have grown fastest of all, more than doubling from 14 per cent of firms in 2023 to 38 per cent in 2026.

items.title: Competence, judgement, diligence the minimum required of licensees
items.teaser: ASIC's finding that former InterPrac boss Garry Crole was neither fit and proper nor competent, and lacked diligence and judgement, is a timely warning: licensee leadership isn't always what advisers assume.
items.brief_text: ASIC’s statement this week that it considered the former chief executive officer and managing director of Sequoia Financial Group – who was also a director and responsible manager of its InterPrac licensee – was neither a fit and proper person nor competent is a timely warning to all advisers that there may be more than meets the eye when it comes to assessing the quality of a licensee’s management. In banning Crole for 10 years from “from performing, as a director or responsible manager, any function involved in carrying on a financial services business”, ASIC said that he “lacked the diligence and judgement required to perform one or more functions as an officer of an entity carrying on a financial services business”. It is a damning assessment of someone carrying out a role that is, frankly, all about diligence, judgement and competence. If you were to sit down and list out the key characteristics of a professional – in any field – those would be at or very close to the top of the list. Maybe you’d add “ethical” to it; ASIC delivered no judgement on that specific issue. Advisers authorised by InterPrac were entitled to expect their licensee’s leadership to be at least fit and proper and competent. Why they didn’t know that it wasn’t is a question only they can answer. Diligence is another issue, and perhaps that was a plus for some InterPrac advisers. But maybe a “light-touch” licensee isn’t all it’s cracked up to be.

items.title: Opposition and peak SMSF body call for a stop to tinkering with rules
items.teaser: Four substantive changes in just five months has led the Shadow Minister for Financial Services Kevin Hogan to call on the government to quit tinkering with the rules. His plea for greater stability and certainty is supported by the peak SMSF industry body.
items.brief_text: The chief executive of the peak self-managed super fund industry body has backed calls by the Shadow Minister for Financial Servies Kevin Hogan for the government to quit tinkering with the rules and provide the sector with greater stability and certainty on how funds are structured, administered and invest. Hogan said in a statement on Thursday that the government has substantively changed the rules for SMSFs four times in just five months. It has introduced the Division 296 tax changes and a higher effective tax rate on the capital gains of super funds that hold their assets indirectly through managed funds such as ETFs, banned SMSFs from borrowing to buy residential property, and last month introduced mandatory trustee education, a written investment strategy, a new ATO veto power over people moving their money into an SMSF, adviser disclosure, and a new CSLR levy contribution. “We don’t know what the education requirement will be, who provides it, or what happens if someone fails. We don’t know in what circumstances the ATO will exercise their new power,” Hogan said. “That’s concerning when the Prime Minister is calling your super a ‘national asset’ to be directed into pet projects like social housing or green energy.” “The 1.2 million Australians with an SMSF don’t want special treatment. They just want stability.

Spanning licensing decisions and risk advice, Andrew explains how being independent influences how he chooses the right professionals to partner with as referral arrangements become more challenging and more necessary by operating as independent. Listen as they discuss: What it actually means to be independent under the Corps Act. How you can still deliver risk advice without breeching independence. items.title: Interdependency and the ATO: A tale of two views
items.teaser: Hallinan said the primary issue of whether the relationship between the adult child and the parent is one which is a “close personal relationship” but more importantly whether that relationship exhibits a “strong commitment to a shared life”.
items.brief_text: Hallinan said the primary issue of whether the relationship between the adult child and the parent is one which is a “close personal relationship” but more importantly whether that relationship exhibits a “strong commitment to a shared life”. “Defining interdependency has four requirements and each must be satisfied for an interdependency relationship to exist. They are domestic support and personal care, financial support, living together and a close personal relationship,” he said, “Can an adult child and a parent be in an interdependency relationship? In the view of the ATO it seems highly unlikely as the ATO considers that an adult child and a parent cannot satisfy the ‘close personal relationship’ requirement of an ‘interdependency relationship’. The ATO seems to identify a ‘close personal relationship’ as being equivalent to a mutual commitment to having a shared life above and beyond that of a parent/child relationship.” However, Hallinan questioned whether the ATO’s view is supported by the relevant legislation. He said the term “interdependency relationship” is defined in section 302-200 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 and has an identical definition in the Superannuation Industry (Supervision) Act 1993. “The Tax Act determines the taxation treatment of a death benefit while the SIS Act determines whether the death benefit can be paid as an income stream,” he said.

items.title: AI boom to drive long-term growth, but it won’t be linear
items.teaser: AI-related technology stocks have enjoyed a meteoric rise over the past three and half years, leading to questions about the sustainability of the AI cycle and the best way for investors to tap into the growth opportunity.
items.brief_text: Produced in partnership with iShares by BlackRock. There are many things keeping investors up at night, including geopolitical uncertainty, trade conflicts and inflation. Another big question is, how much longer there is to go on the artificial intelligence (AI) mega trend, given that it has already been running for over three and a half years. Since late 2022, when OpenAI launched ChatGPT 3.5, AI-related companies have become the dominant force in equity markets. BlackRock analysis shows that AI-related companies represent 47 per cent of market cap but drive 67 per cent of total earnings growth. For cautious investors who haven’t dived in yet, the concern is that they may be too late. For early movers who have been riding the AI theme higher and higher, the concern is that all the exuberance and money pouring into the sector could be creating a bubble. According to Lydia Vitalis, director, Australia investment strategy at BlackRock, the AI thematic is a long-term play that is reshaping the investment opportunity set and driving future returns, although performance is unlikely to be linear. “Technology stocks have performed very strongly, and we think this will continue [VL1] [LO2] , although the opportunity is moving beyond the initial excitement of a narrow technology story to a broader infrastructure and productivity story,” she says.

items.title: Nasdaq leadership enters its next phase
items.teaser: AI-led earnings growth and a historic investment cycle continue to place the Nasdaq’s largest companies at the centre of global equity markets.
items.brief_text: Produced in partnership with iShares by BlackRock. AI-led earnings growth and a historic investment cycle continue to place the Nasdaq’s largest companies at the centre of global equity markets. But for advisers, the question is increasingly not whether to participate in the theme, but how much concentration is appropriate – and where the next phase of returns may come from. US earnings continue to provide support for the AI-led equity story. As of early August, around 75 per cent of US companies had beaten Q2 earnings expectations, with aggregate earnings beat of approximately 8 per cent. AI-linked companies accounted for more than 65 per cent of earnings growth, while non-AI companies also recorded an average 6 per cent upward earnings revision through reporting season.[1] That strength builds on a sustained period of US market leadership. Over the five years to 31 July 2026, US equities outperformed Australian shares by around 5 per cent a year, while the more technology-heavy Nasdaq-100 delivered roughly 7 per cent more per year than the Australian market in AUD terms.[2] [3] BlackRock expects the US earnings backdrop to remain constructive, with analysis pointing to earnings growth of around 11.6 per cent a year over the next five years – a pace historically observed in only around 15 per cent of five-year periods.[4] This remains an important support for US equities and the broader AI investment theme.

items.title: Investors price more risk into listed private credit trusts: Morningstar
items.teaser: Investors are pricing in more risk for listed private credit vehicles, which are structured as listed investment trusts (LITs), with some trusts trading at a discount of 25% of their net asset value (NAV), according to Morningstar.
items.brief_text: Investors are pricing in more risk for listed private credit vehicles, which are structured as listed investment trusts (LITs), with some trusts trading at a discount of 25% of their net asset value (NAV), according to Morningstar. Property developer Bathla Group went into voluntary administration in late August, raising fears that investors will pull back from private credit funds exposed to the property sector. According to Morningstar data, as of July 31, Metrics Real Estate Multi-Strategy Fund was trading at 27.2% discount of NAV. Metrics' Income Opportunities Trust also sat at a 23.3% discount, while KKR's Credit Income Fund traded at a discount of 13.3%. Morningstar director of manager research Thomas Dutka notes that the performance of LITs is a proxy for investor sentiment into the sector. "For a number of these funds, there have been some fairly sizeable reductions in their trading value. These aren't necessarily funds exposed to Bathla," Dutka told Financial Standard . "Some of the factors driving the declines are probably going to be more linked directly to some of the issues that have been reported in relation to those funds." ASIC has been scrutinising Australia's private credit sector , calling on funds to ensure their asset valuations are current, accurate and grounded in realistic assumptions.

items.title: Openmarkets taps $22tn tokenised market
items.teaser: Openmarkets Group and Ondo Finance will bring the latter's institutional-grade tokenised financial products to eligible Australian investors, developing new products tailored to the local market.
items.brief_text: Openmarkets Group and Ondo Finance will bring the latter's institutional-grade tokenised financial products to eligible Australian investors, developing new products tailored to the local market. Both organisations have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to bring together Ondo's global tokenisation capabilities and Openmarkets' local market expertise and financial infrastructure. Specifically, the partnership will assess pathways for Openmarkets to distribute selected Ondo products, while exploring tokenised products and market infrastructure tailored to local investors, potentially including tokenised Australian-listed securities and access to offshore tokenised markets, the parties said. The MoU comes amid many organisations not yet willing to make the first step to expand into digital finance due to several factors highlighted by BlockchainAPAC during its recent national roadshow in Australia. One of these is the "first-mover costs" that are holding back investment even though technology is no longer the principal barrier. Meanwhile, the government recently passed the Digital Asset Framework Bill to mandate digital asset exchanges and platforms to carry an AFSL . Openmarkets carries an AFSL and recently expanded its operations into private wealth advisory .

items.title: Mining, property fuel Aussie billionaires' wealth
items.teaser: Australian billionaires' riches are highly concentrated in mining, financial services, technology and property, accounting for 0.7% of the total US$15.1 trillion in global wealth studied by the 2026 Billionaire Census.
items.brief_text: Australian billionaires' riches are highly concentrated in mining, financial services, technology and property, accounting for 0.7% of the total US$15.1 trillion in global wealth studied by the 2026 Billionaire Census. Global wealth intelligence provider Altrata found Australia dominates the Pacific region when it comes to the billionaire population. In the last year, Australia's billionaire population rose modestly in absolute number to 51 individuals, on the back of global demand for mineral commodities and financial and business services, the report found. However, wealth gains were constrained by subdued export trends to China and real estate pressures that dampened equity-market returns. Asia, the third-largest billionaire region, recorded a 6.5% rise in its billionaire population to 881 individuals. The increase in wealth was driven by the positive spillover effects of the wider artificial investment (AI) investment boom, supportive fiscal and governance reforms, and global investor diversification underpinned strong returns in many of the region's equity markets. South Korea's tech-heavy KOSPI index was the top global performer, with robust gains also in Taiwan, Japan, and Hong Kong, the report read. In contrast, returns in the fast-growing billionaire market of India were relatively muted for a second consecutive year. New York continues to be the global billionaire capital with an 8% rise in billionaire numbers to 164.

items.title: Natixis IM adds Mirova private assets team in Sydney
items.teaser: Natixis Investment Managers affiliate Mirova has launched a dedicated private assets team in Sydney. The new team will initially consist of three professionals, including Kim Nguyen as an investment director, and an unnamed investment manager and investment analyst.
items.brief_text: Natixis Investment Managers affiliate Mirova has launched a dedicated private assets team in Sydney. The new team will initially consist of three professionals, including Kim Nguyen as an investment director, and an unnamed investment manager and investment analyst. Nguyen most recently served as executive director, investments at the NSW Government’s Energy Security Corporation and previously led Foresight Group’s Australian business. The trio will sit within Natixis IM Australia, a Sydney outpost of the Paris-headquartered firm which first opened in 2007. Together, they will focus on originating, evaluating and supporting investments for Mirova’s Energy Transition Infrastructure platform, as well as deepening relationships with local investors, developers, and industry stakeholders. It comes as Natixis IM says Australia has become a key destination for Mirova’s energy transition investments. Via its Asia Pacific hub in Singapore, Mirova has already deployed more than $700 million across Australia and New Zealand in recent years. This includes stakes in businesses such as clean energy firm TagEnergy, EV charging specialist JET Charge, and renewables company Yanara Australia. Natixis IM cited the country’s renewable energy resources, growing infrastructure pipeline, supportive policy environment and increasing demand for private capital to fund the energy transition as drawcards for investment.

items.title: FEATURE | Digital advice | Interlocking the pieces
items.teaser: Digital advice has become a core offering for wealth managers, yet it confuses many and implementation and use remain fragmented. Before it can achieve aspirations of scale, experts are urging for a better, unified understanding of the offering.
items.brief_text: Amid a rapidly evolving regulatory space, and the need to keep pace with innovation, financial advice has been thrown into a dynamic environment that's always changing. As a result, the sector requires constant support to remain compliant and keep on top of those changes. Digital advice is emerging, with many super funds and advisers using these tools to scale and improve efficiency. However, digital advice isn't as simple as implementing artificial intelligence (AI) into an adviser's daily operations, and this misconception continues to play out over the years. AZ NGA group chief executive Paul Barrett says although digital advice has been available for a little over a decade, it is still in its "infancy" in terms of how engagement is going to play a role in the future, highlighting that there's still a long way to go to extrapolate the full potential of digital advice. Currently, providers are trying to build better apps to engage clients directly so as to prompt people at the right time in their financial life cycle and therefore seek advice. Then and there is the "old school concept of "robo-advice" that he explains as just a "dressed-up managed funds implementation business." "There's a huge opportunity for advice businesses to spend more money engaging their clients using AI and other digital means, but to do that, you firstly need scale," he says.

items.title: GQG Partners sees year of consecutive monthly outflows
items.teaser: Investors are yet to be convinced by GQG’s pivot back into technology with outflows continuing through August. In its monthly funds under management (FUM) update, it saw US$4.3 billion ($6 billion) in outflows during August which is its second-highest monthly outflows since the start of the year.
items.brief_text: Investors are yet to be convinced by GQG’s pivot back into technology with outflows continuing through August. In its monthly funds under management (FUM) update, it saw US$4.3 billion ($6 billion) in outflows during August which is its second-highest monthly outflows since the start of the year. This followed US$4.5 billion in July and US$3.2 billion in June with every month seeing outflows for the past 12 months, much of which has been attributed to its avoidance of AI. While some monthly outflows have been offset by positive investment performance, this was not the case for August where it reported -US$2.9 billion thanks to investment performance. This meant FUM fell from US$156.4 billion at the start of the month to US$149.2 billion and from US$163.9 billion at the start of the year. items.title: Active ETF launches push ETF products past 500

items.brief_text: The number of ETFs available in Australia has surpassed 500 after 11 were added in August, according to Betashares. The product volume now stands at a total of 505 ETFs after 11 ETFs were launched during the month. Launches during August included State Street’s first two active ETFs in Australia in partnership with Blackstone, four from Betashares, three from VanEck and one each from JP Morgan Asset Management and Vanguard. August launches: JPMorgan Australia Equity Active ETF Betashares Diversified High Growth ETF Betashares Diversified Growth ETF Betashares Diversified Balanced ETF Betashares Diversified Credit Income ETF State Street Blackstone Senior Loan (AUD Hedged) Active ETF State Street Blackstone High Income (AUD Hedged) Active ETF Vanguard Australian Floating Rate Bond ETF VanEck Global Semiconductor ETF VanEck Quantum ETF VanEck Rare Earth and Strategic Metals ex-China ETF The largest ETF currently available in Australia is the Vanguard Australian Shares Index ETF which sits at more than $26 billion. Betashares’ monthly report found $7 billion was poured into ETFs during August, beating the $6.8 billion seen in the previous month. This brings the market cap to $382 billion, on track to reach $400 billion by year-end. International equities were the most-popular category with $3.8 billion going into these ETFs.

items.title: Death, incapacity and the auditor’s role
items.teaser: Speaking at the SMSF Association Audit Day, Burrows said there are key objectives SMSF auditors should always be considering and they need to identify where the risks are especially when dealing with death and incapacity as it is then that the risks can be greater.
items.brief_text: Speaking at the SMSF Association Audit Day, Burrows said there are key objectives SMSF auditors should always be considering and they need to identify where the risks are especially when dealing with death and incapacity as it is then that the risks can be greater. “We need to understand the documents, evaluate the evidence, fulfill our obligations to the auditing standards, the ethical requirements, the SIS Act, and report to the ATO and trustee if necessary,” he said. “And you have to ensure your audit file stands up to review. These are all really important points, but I wanted to emphasise the last one in particular. You can perform the greatest audit, have considered all the key points, but if the documents are not in your audit file, or an external party can’t follow the work that you’ve done, it’s as if you haven’t done it.” Burrows said if the ATO does review an audit file, it will do so against its own assessment of how it believes the auditing standards apply. Additionally, audit file expectations have been entered into case law through more recent Administrative Review Tribunal decisions. “ The contents of your audit file is crucial, and you don’t want it questioned by a disgruntled beneficiary,” he said. He continued that using an evidence-first framework can help ensure that an audit file has covered all contingencies.
